notes.meaning: Abimelech travels to Shechem, the hometown of his mother, to plot with his maternal relatives. His father Gideon had refused to be king, but Abimelech wants the crown for himself. He uses his family ties in Shechem to build support for his personal ambition.

Abimelech tells his relatives to ask the city leaders whether it is better to have seventy rulers or just one. He falsely suggests that all of Gideon's other sons want to rule over them, which was not true. He then appeals to local pride by reminding them that he is their own flesh and blood.

Abimelech's uncles present this proposal to the leaders of Shechem, and the leaders readily agree to back him. They decide to support him simply because he is their relative, hoping his rise will bring honor and advantage to their own city. Selfish motives often blind people to what is right.

The leaders give Abimelech seventy pieces of silver from the temple treasury of Baal-berith, the local covenant idol. Abimelech uses this idol money to hire reckless, unemployed men to serve as his private gang. A movement funded by false gods and led by criminals cannot please the Lord.

Abimelech leads his men to his father's house in Ophrah and brutally murders his seventy half-brothers on a single stone. This cruel slaughter was meant to eliminate any potential rivals to his rule. Only Jotham, Gideon's youngest son, survives because he managed to hide.

The leaders of Shechem and the nearby stronghold gather at the sacred oak and crown Abimelech as their king. They do this without asking God, who had never called Abimelech to lead His people. Instead of punishing a mass murderer, they reward him with royal power.

When Jotham hears what happened, he climbs to a cliff on Mount Gerizim and shouts down to the leaders of Shechem below. He demands that they listen to his warning so that God might hear their cries in the future. Mount Gerizim was the ancient hill where God's blessings had been read, making Jotham's speech especially powerful.

Jotham begins a fable about the trees looking for a king to rule over them. They first turn to the olive tree, asking it to accept the throne. Anointing with oil was the sacred custom used to set apart a king for his office.

The olive tree refuses the crown, asking why it should abandon its rich oil just to wave back and forth over the other trees. Olive oil was used to honor God in tabernacle offerings and to honor people in anointings and daily meals. A truly useful servant of God will not give up doing good just to chase worldly status.
Next, the trees approach the fig tree and invite it to become their king. Like the olive, the fig tree was known throughout Israel as a valuable source of food and blessing.

The fig tree turns them down as well, refusing to give up its sweet and good fruit just to take on the burdens of kingship. It preferred producing quiet nourishment over holding an empty title of power.
The trees then invite the grapevine to come and rule over them. The vine was another essential plant in Israel that provided refreshment and joy for the community.

The grapevine refuses, unwilling to stop producing wine that cheers both God in sacred drink offerings and people at their tables. Like the other fruit trees, it refuses to trade its fruitful calling for the anxious cares of ruling.

Having been turned down by every productive tree, all the trees finally ask the worthless thornbush to rule over them. The thornbush produces no edible fruit, has no pleasant shade, and is covered with sharp spikes. It represents Abimelech, a cruel and useless man eager to grab power for himself.

The thornbush accepts the offer and invites the trees to find shelter in its meager shade. It immediately threatens that if they are not truly loyal, fire will burst out of its brambles and burn down even the mighty cedars of Lebanon. A tyrant promises protection he cannot deliver and threatens total destruction against anyone who opposes him.

Jotham turns the fable directly upon his listeners, asking if they have acted with honesty and integrity in making Abimelech king. He questions whether they have shown proper gratitude and honor to the memory of his father Gideon. An ungodly act can never be justified by pretending to have good motives.

Jotham reminds them that his father Gideon risked his very life to rescue Israel from the cruel Midianites. Instead of repaying that sacrifice with loyalty, the men of Shechem helped murder Gideon's seventy sons on a single stone and crowned a concubine's son simply because he was their relative. Betraying those who defended you is a terrible wickedness in God's sight.

Jotham says that if they have truly acted righteously toward Gideon's household, they are welcome to rejoice in Abimelech, and he in them. He speaks with sharp irony, knowing their consciences are guilty of murder and betrayal. True joy never comes from alliances built on deceit.

Jotham warns that if they have acted unjustly, fire will break out from Abimelech and consume the leaders of Shechem, and fire will break out from Shechem to destroy Abimelech. This was a prophecy that their wicked partnership would end in mutual slaughter. Those who join together in evil will eventually tear each other apart.

After finishing his warning, Jotham flees for his life to the town of Beer. He settles there in exile because he knows his brother Abimelech would try to hunt him down. God protected Jotham so that his words of judgment could stand as a witness.

Abimelech manages to rule over the central region of Israel for three years. The people had tolerated his violent rise to power because of their own longing for a king. His brief reign was marked by oppressive tyranny rather than the godly care of a true judge.

God sends a spirit of bitterness and distrust between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, leading the citizens to turn treacherous against him. Their former friendship collapses into jealousy, suspicion, and secret plotting. God easily shatters wicked partnerships when the time for judgment arrives.

God allowed this strife so that justice would be served for the murder of Gideon's seventy sons. Both Abimelech, who committed the murders, and the leaders of Shechem, who paid for the crime, were held guilty for shedding innocent blood. God's justice may seem delayed, but evil deeds will always be answered.

The leaders of Shechem set up ambushes along the mountain roads to rob travelers and disrupt Abimelech's control over the region. By doing this, they undermined his authority and kept trade revenue away from him. When Abimelech hears about their lawlessness, he knows open rebellion has begun.

A raider named Gaal arrives in Shechem with his company of men, looking for an opportunity to gain power. Sensing the growing anger toward Abimelech, Gaal offers his services to the city, and the leaders place their trust in him. Rebellious people often put their hope in reckless new leaders when trying to escape an old tyrant.

Feeling protected by Gaal's forces, the people finally go out to harvest their grapes and tread the winepresses. They hold a drunken festival inside the temple of their idol, Baal-berith, to celebrate their harvest and their newfound boldness. As they drink and feast before their false god, they openly curse Abimelech.

Emboldened by wine, Gaal brags before the crowd and mocks Abimelech's right to rule over them. He argues that Abimelech is only the son of Gideon, the man who tore down Baal's altar, while leaving Zebul as an outside governor over the city. Gaal urges the people to abandon Abimelech and serve the ancient Canaanite line of Hamor, the founder of Shechem.
